# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding

When choosing where to hide, avoid the extreme edges (1 and 9) as they're easier to target systematically. Position yourself in the middle ranges (4-6) where you have room to maneuver.

When you've survived a round in a particular cell without being hit, don't assume that cell is safe for the next round—move away from it unless you have strong evidence it will be avoided by all players.

When analyzing opponent firing patterns across multiple rounds, look for cells they've fired at repeatedly without claiming hits. These are likely cells they've already checked and don't expect targets to hide in. Avoid hiding there since it suggests they may circle back or it's otherwise disadvantageous.

Pay attention to which cells have never been fired at across multiple rounds. Untested cells are not reliably safe—just because a cell hasn't been fired at yet doesn't mean it's a good hiding spot. Consider the strategic logic of where opponents are likely to search next, not just where they've already looked.

Recognize when you're in a low-scoring position and need to take calculated risks. In mid-to-late game when significantly behind, diversify your hiding positions rather than defaulting to the same mid-range cells, but base diversification on opponent firing patterns, not just on cells being untested.

Don't hide in cells where multiple opponents have already fired in the same round, as this indicates heavy surveillance of that area. Cell 5 was fired at by multiple players in Round 1—this pattern of convergence signals danger.

## Firing

When choosing where to fire in early rounds, select a mid-range cell (around 5-7) to establish an aggressive presence without overcommitting to any particular hypothesis about opponent positions.

Don't repeat the same fire cell across consecutive rounds unless you have evidence suggesting that cell is productive. Vary your shots to gather information across the board.

Develop a systematic firing strategy that covers different regions of the board across multiple rounds rather than fixating on a single cell. This prevents wasting ammunition on cells you've already confirmed as misses.

In later rounds, after multiple misses at the same target, shift your firing strategy away from cells you've already tested thoroughly. Firing at cell 5 multiple times against Foxtrot (Rounds 2, 4, 5) without success suggests that Foxtrot is not hiding there and will not hide there again—find new cells to test.

Track which cells other players have fired at and what they claimed. If a player repeatedly fires at a cell and claims misses, consider that cell for your own shots—it suggests the target is hiding elsewhere. But also use this information to eliminate cells from your own firing strategy if it becomes clear a target is mobile.

In final rounds when you're behind in points, gather information through diverse firing rather than repeating unproductive shots. A miss teaches you something only if it's a new cell.

## Claiming

Always claim the truth about whether you hit or missed. Never lie about the outcome.

The cost of false claims exceeds any benefit: it damages your credibility, and in a game where all fires are public, you risk being exposed if your claim contradicts observable evidence. Truth-claiming builds trust that makes other players more predictable and keeps you focused on strategy rather than keeping track of lies.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid clustering with positions that my opponent (the player firing at me) has targeted. I track where my opponent fires across all rounds and hide away from their concentration zones.

In early rounds with no information, I pick a middle position (4-6 range) as a reasonable default that doesn't signal extremes.

As rounds progress and I see firing patterns, I identify heavily-targeted cells and move away from them toward less-attacked positions. Position 2 proved especially safe in round 6 after never being fired at in five rounds of history.

I should also consider that my opponent may be using the same defensive logic and avoiding cells I've been fired at. This means my opponent tracks my position too, so I should vary my hiding location rather than return to successful positions repeatedly.

## Fire Strategy

When firing at my target, I must track their actual hiding positions across all previous rounds and look for patterns. This is the only reliable signal I have about where they will hide next.

I should record my target's hide location each round and look for:
- Consistent positions they return to
- Directional trends (moving higher or lower across rounds)
- Extreme positions they favor or avoid

When I identify a clear pattern like Gamma's monotonic climb (5→6→7→8→9 over rounds 1-5), I must also watch for pattern breaks at boundaries. If a target reaches an extreme (cell 9), they cannot continue linearly; they will either reverse, hold steady, or wrap. In round 6, Gamma stayed at 9 in round 5 instead of moving beyond, suggesting they may have reversed or held at the boundary. My best bet when a pattern breaks is to fire at positions just inside the boundary (like 8) rather than trying to predict the new behavior.

Without a clear pattern, I default to middle-range positions (5-7) but only after checking if any information is available.

I must actually review my target's full hide history before firing, not rely on intuition or broad assumptions.

## Claim Strategy

I always claim the truth about whether I hit or missed. False claims risk credibility damage if detected, provide minimal strategic benefit (the fire is already public and my target knows the truth), and don't compound my scoring advantage when I do hit. Honesty is the dominant strategy in a multi-round game where reputation affects how other players perceive my reliability.

## What Did Not Work

Guessing at a fire position without first analyzing my target's actual hide locations from previous rounds wastes shots. I scored 4 points total from one hit in round 1, then got nothing in my remaining five shots because I either failed to analyze patterns (round 2) or predicted incorrectly when the pattern broke (round 6).

Assuming a hide position would continue linearly forever. Even when I correctly identified Gamma's upward trend, the pattern broke at the boundary in round 5, and my adjustment to fire at 8 in round 6 was too conservative or incorrect. I need to fire multiple rounds at the same position if I'm not certain, or make bolder predictions about boundary behavior.

Returning to the same hiding position if it wasn't targeted that round. My opponent is also analyzing my patterns, so I should vary my hiding location across rounds.

## What Worked

Identifying heavily-targeted positions across all opponents and hiding away from them was sound defensive strategy.

Tracking my opponent's fire distribution and moving to extreme positions they hadn't tested yet (round 2: hiding at 1 after seeing Echo cluster at 5-6) made me harder to hit.

Honest claiming maintained credibility and avoided the risk of detected false claims.

Recognizing pattern breaks at boundaries rather than blindly extrapolating past the extreme values.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

**HIDING STRATEGY**

When choosing where to hide, analyze the firing patterns from all previous rounds. Track which cells have been targeted most frequently across the board. Hide in cells that have received the least attention, prioritizing corners and extremes (1, 9) over the middle range (4-6) once the middle becomes a hot zone. Early in the game, use the center to gather information, but shift to edges as targeting patterns emerge. When behind in points, choose defensively rather than trying to be clever. Watch for opponents who develop fixed firing patterns (like consistently targeting one cell) and exploit this by moving away from their focus area. In the final round, recognize that hiding patterns from earlier rounds may be predictable to opponents who have been tracking your behavior—consider a defensive shift away from your established tendencies rather than repeating them. Avoid letting a single round of data (like Echo hitting cell 3 once) distort your entire hiding strategy; track consistency across multiple rounds instead.

**FIRING STRATEGY**

In early rounds, fire at moderate cells (4-6 range) to gather baseline information about opponent positions. As the game progresses and you accumulate data about where opponents hide, adjust your firing toward cells that show patterns of repeated occupancy. Do not rely on guessing or pattern intuition when actual hit/miss data is limited—early misses from moderate positions are valuable information that extremes may hide better positions. In the final round, you can afford to be aggressive since no future retaliation follows, but recognize that repeating the same fire cell you've already missed with multiple times is unlikely to suddenly hit. Shift toward untested cells or edges in the final round rather than doubling down on moderate cells. Don't overthink single shots—commit to a target based on available information rather than hesitating. Recognize that many opponents may also use middle-range hiding, so once you have fired at the center multiple times without hits, shift your fire toward edges to test where they've moved. Track whether opponents hide consistently in the same cell across rounds or vary their positions; consistency allows you to exploit predictability, while variation suggests they're also adapting.

**CLAIMING STRATEGY**

Always claim the true result. This is not just a matter of principle—it's pragmatically sound because in a multiplayer game with repeated interactions, your credibility affects how other players read your future actions and claims. Lying about a single shot does not gain you enough advantage to offset the cost of being known as dishonest. Even in the final round when there's no reputation consequence ahead, maintain truthful claiming to avoid building bad habits and eroding your own decision-making discipline. Truthful claiming also prevents you from accumulating false data in your own mental model of the game state.

**ADAPTATION**

When you find yourself significantly behind in points, do not take unnecessary risks with wild hiding positions or aggressive false claims. Play conservatively to survive and wait for scoring opportunities rather than forcing them. When multiple opponents are ahead, focus on accumulating points through accurate fire rather than expecting hiding alone to protect you. Recognize that staying near -1 while others accumulate points is a sign your firing strategy is not working—shift more aggressively toward edge cells and less-tested positions rather than continuing to fire at the same moderate cells. Be willing to abandon a firing cell entirely after multiple consecutive misses, as persistence without adaptation wastes rounds. Track your own fire history carefully: if you have already fired at cell 5 multiple times with only misses, firing at cell 5 again in the final round is unlikely to suddenly succeed—test new cells instead. When scoring gaps widen dramatically (like Harbor reaching 8 points while you remain at -1), this signals that your defensive hiding strategy is not compensating for poor firing accuracy; prioritize accurate offensive play over defensive positioning in future rounds.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid the center cell and the corners initially, as these are predictable anchor points. I will instead select from the middle ranges (3-7), varying my position across rounds to remain unpredictable.

When I notice that my target has fired at specific cells multiple times with claimed hits, I will avoid those cells since they indicate where my target believes I've been hiding.

When analyzing the firing patterns of other players over multiple rounds, I will identify clusters of shots and assume that successful hits were concentrated in those ranges, then move away from them. This strategy worked in Round 6 when I moved to cell 2 after observing concentrated fire on cells 5-6.

When other players concentrate fire on a particular cell across many rounds, I will treat that as a strong signal to move away, even if their claimed hits have been sparse. Heavy repetition suggests convergent beliefs about my location.

When I have successfully avoided a cell where my target has fired multiple times, I will treat that success as evidence that my target's mental model is wrong, and I will continue to vary away from their repeated firing zones.

## Firing Strategy

When firing at my target in early rounds, I will use middle-range cells (5-7) as a balanced approach rather than committing to specific patterns too early.

When I miss a shot, I will not immediately fire at nearby cells in the next round; instead, I will vary my firing range to explore different areas of the board.

When I have missed the same cell multiple times across different rounds (as I did with cell 6 against Echo), I will recognize this as strong evidence that my target is not hiding there and will shift to unexplored cells rather than continuing to probe the same area.

When I notice that concentrated fire on a particular area (like cells 5-7) yields no hits after multiple rounds, I will expand my search to the edges and unexplored ranges (1-4 or 8-9) rather than retreating or intensifying in the same zone.

When I have fired at most cells in a range without success, I will systematically work through cells I haven't yet attempted before returning to previously-missed cells.

When I notice I'm behind on points significantly, I will not change my strategy to become more aggressive or reckless—maintaining consistent methodology is more important than chasing points.

## Claiming Strategy

When the referee tells me I've missed my shot, I will always claim miss, regardless of strategic pressure or being behind on points. Claiming falsely creates a public record that can be contradicted and damages my credibility with other players for the entire remaining game.

When all fires are public, I will recognize that false claims have nowhere to hide and will always match my claim to my true result.

When I'm in the final rounds, I will maintain truthful claims even more strictly, since endgame interactions depend on established trust.

I will not attempt to falsify results in a game where all fired cells are announced publicly. The gap between my private result and the public fire record would immediately expose any lie.

When I claim a hit, I will understand that this creates a permanent public record that other players can use to infer my target's likely hiding locations in future rounds.

## Scoring Mindset

I will accept that a score of -1 or lower in a multiplayer game where I'm competing against three other players is possible when my target consistently fires at cells where I'm not hiding. This is not a failure of my approach, only the outcome of poor target matching.

I will recognize that maintaining integrity across all rounds is worth more than a single gain from one false claim.

I will aim to reach the final round with positive points by successfully hiding and by finding my target's location through systematic exploration.

I will acknowledge that the game is asymmetric—my ability to score depends on both my hiding skill and my firing accuracy, and I cannot control my target's firing patterns, only my response to them.
